topics.topic: Disposal of unread request-body bytes and conditions for connection reuse
questions: If a handler answers or refuses without consuming the stream to its end, does the listener drain the remaining framed body, close the connection, or permit reuse only after the reader explicitly discards it?
When a surface answers without consuming the entire body, who disposes of the unread bytes, and is the connection drained, closed, or eligible for another request?
If a surface does not read all of a request body, what happens to the unread bytes and the connection before another request can be accepted on it?

judgement.why: This is the same question about unread bodies, connection persistence, sequencing and reuse limits already assigned to State 4 by P2.

precedent.topic: Connection persistence, pipelining, sequencing, ordering, and reuse limits
quotes:
The reading and writing of its wire format. The HTTP server, its
connections and HTTP's framing are `instance_lifecycle`'s listener's, as for
the owner interface.
precedent.why: Connection persistence, pipelining, dispatch sequencing and response ordering are flow questions owned by State 4.

topics.topic: Exact malformed HTTP request-framing header forms
questions: Exactly which header combinations and values are malformed, including duplicate `Content-Length`, both headers together, repeated `Transfer-Encoding`, transfer codings other than `chunked`, and a missing framing header?

Exactly which header forms are malformed, including repeated or conflicting `Content-Length`, simultaneous `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding`, unsupported transfer codings, coding lists, overflow and non-canonical numeric forms?

Which exact header forms are malformed, including duplicate `Content-Length` fields, comma-separated values, simultaneous `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding`, transfer codings other than `chunked`, and `chunked` not being the final coding?

judgement.why: The exact accepted grammar and combinations of HTTP framing headers are wire-encoding and contract details owned by State 6, while State 3 already assigns their parsing to instance_lifecycle.

topics.topic: HTTP response and connection disposition after a body-framing stream failure
questions: After that failure, does Registry send an HTTP error response or close without an answer, and must it close the connection?
Must every body-stream framing failure close the connection, or may the listener attempt to recover and serve another request on it?
When that failure occurs, is an HTTP error response sent or is the connection closed without an answer, and must the connection always become unusable?

quotes:
the body itself is never read
ahead by the listener, so a body that ends before its framing says, or
whose chunks are malformed, is a failure of the stream its reader sees
while reading it;
judgement.why: Recovery, response production and subsequent connection use after a stream failure are flow and sequencing questions owned by State 4.

topics.topic: Meaning and permitted buffering boundary of the listener's no-read-ahead rule
questions: Does this prohibit only application-level consumption before a surface reads, or also socket, TLS and HTTP-library buffering of body bytes, and how much data may be buffered?
Does “never read ahead” forbid only eager consumption before handing the stream to a surface, or also socket/library buffering and draining performed on demand after the surface returns?

Does “never read ahead” forbid all body reads until the surface pulls, permit bounded buffering within the current framed body, or only forbid reading beyond that body's boundary into the next request?

judgement.why: This is the same listener-to-surface stream-contract question P3 assigned to State 6, including the exact buffering and cancellation semantics.

precedent.topic: HTTP request parsing ownership and the listener-to-surface request contract
quotes:
The reading and writing of its wire format. The HTTP server, its
connections and HTTP's framing are `instance_lifecycle`'s listener's, as for
the owner interface.

each request's body handed on as a stream that ends where HTTP's own
framing ends the body — after its `Content-Length` bytes, or at the last
chunk of a chunked body — so that no reader of it waits for bytes the client
sends only after an answer, and no byte of another request is read as the
body's —
precedent.why: State 3 assigns HTTP framing to instance_lifecycle and application wire decoding to service_api; the exact request object, header representation, stream errors and cancellation are contract and signature details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Ownership, location, translation, and dependency direction of the body-stream framing-failure contract
questions: What concrete failure does the stream expose, and which module owns the failure type and translates it into request handling?

Which module owns the stream-failure type and its handling: `instance_lifecycle`, the reading `service_api` or `owner_interface` module, or another transport abstraction, and in which direction does that dependency run?
Which module owns the stream failure's type and contract, and which module must translate it into request failure: `instance_lifecycle`, `service_api`, or `owner_interface`?
Where can the shared body-stream and framing-failure contract live without making `service_api` and `owner_interface` depend back on their facade, which already depends on and delegates to them?

quotes:
The request's raw body is another port of
`models` with the same one method, `ByteStream`, which is `external`: the
HTTP server makes it, and `owner_interface` takes it as such.

A
  stream that ends before the delimiter makes its `read` raise, a failure of
  the stream that `read_import_mapping` answers `file_unreadable`, as any
  stream that fails;
judgement.why: State 6 places the shared raw-body port in models, makes the HTTP server its external implementation, and states how the upload reader translates a stream failure, avoiding a dependency from either surface back to instance_lifecycle.

topics.topic: Whether operations must await complete body validation and whether earlier state changes may remain after framing failure
questions: Must every handler finish reading and validating all body bytes it needs before making any runtime or durable change, or can effects performed before a later framing failure remain?

What is the operation-level outcome when this failure occurs after the request has reached a surface: must the operation be treated as refused with no state change, may already completed checks or session changes remain, and may an HTTP answer be sent?

Must a surface consume and successfully reach the framed end of every request body before committing an operation, or may it act after parsing the values it needs even though unread framing can later fail?

quotes:
None of its own: it refuses nothing. An operation name that is not one of
A09 rule 2's reaches `operations`, which refuses it at stage (1) as outside
the service's rights (`not_permitted`, `outside_service_rights`), whatever
token it carries once the token is valid; inputs that are not of the wire
format — a body that cannot be read as it, a field it does not declare, a
value of another shape than its field's — are answered stage (1) first and
then `invalid_request` (`outside_closed_list`) at stage (4).

No refusal
carries a digest: a file over the size limit is refused before any of it is
parsed — a declared length over it before any byte is read, otherwise as
soon as more than it has been read; a stream that fails or ends before its
declared length is refused as `file_unreadable`, replacing nothing kept and
changing nothing of the session but the instant of its last request, which
every request carrying it moves (A13 rule 2) — and an
unreadable or malformed one is refused with its kind alone.
judgement.why: State 5 makes an unreadable service body an invalid input rather than an executable change and separately fixes the upload failure's sole surviving session effect and absence of a kept replacement.

topics.topic: Timeout or cancellation policy and ownership for stalled incomplete bodies
questions: What ends a read when the client neither sends the promised bytes nor closes the connection, and which module owns that timeout or cancellation policy?
What ends a request whose headers are valid but whose client neither completes nor terminates the body, and which module owns that timeout or cancellation?

judgement.why: P3 already assigns stream errors and cancellation in the listener-to-surface request contract to State 6, which includes the timeout or cancellation of a stalled body read.

topics.topic: How far a malformed-body request progresses and which pre-discovery request effects may occur
questions: Has a request with malformed body framing already reached `service_api` or `owner_interface`, and which authentication, session-arrival, rate-limit or other request effects may occur before the failure is discovered?

quotes:
An upload arrives, for the session
check, once its head has been read (A13 rule 2).

No refusal
carries a digest: a file over the size limit is refused before any of it is
parsed — a declared length over it before any byte is read, otherwise as
soon as more than it has been read; a stream that fails or ends before its
declared length is refused as `file_unreadable`, replacing nothing kept and
changing nothing of the session but the instant of its last request, which
every request carrying it moves (A13 rule 2) — and an
unreadable or malformed one is refused with its kind alone.
judgement.why: The later operations text says the upload reaches session admission after its head, so a later framing failure is file_unreadable and leaves only the required last-request refresh.
